content: The risk of developing type 1 diabetes is influenced by a genetic predisposition, particularly associated with specific HLA types such as DR3 and DR4. Additionally, an unknown environmental trigger, suspected to be an infection (though no definitive infectious agent has been identified in all cases), and an uncontrolled autoimmune response targeting insulin-producing beta cells are key factors in its development. Some studies suggest that breastfeeding may reduce the risk of type 1 diabetes. Various other nutritional factors are under investigation, but no conclusive evidence has been established. Administering 2000 IU of vitamin D during the first year of life has been associated with a reduced risk of type 1 diabetes. For type 2 diabetes, risk reduction is often achievable through dietary modifications and increased physical activity. The American Diabetes Association (ADA) recommends maintaining a healthy weight, engaging in at least 2.5 hours of exercise per week (such as brisk walking), consuming a diet with moderate fat intake, and incorporating adequate fiber and whole grains. While the ADA does not endorse alcohol consumption as a preventive measure, moderate alcohol intake may reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes, though excessive consumption is clearly harmful to overall health. There is insufficient evidence to support the clinical benefit of consuming foods with a low glycemic index. In individuals predisposed to diabetes, the prophylactic use of medications such as metformin, rosiglitazone, or valsartan has shown some evidence of delaying disease progression. Among patients taking hydroxychloroquine for rheumatoid arthritis, the incidence of diabetes was reduced by 77%. Breastfeeding may also contribute to the prevention of type 2 diabetes in mothers. Adequate copper intake might play a role in preventing insulin-dependent diabetes, as it has shown protective effects in animal models, such as ATZ-poisoned mice. Copper in drinking water has demonstrated some protective effects, potentially through its role in superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity. Metalloporphyrin-based SOD has been shown to prevent or delay the onset of autoimmune cascades in diabetes in mice. However, significant differences between human and animal models suggest that this remains a theoretical possibility rather than a proven intervention. In children with diabetes-related antibodies, treatment with vitamin B3 (niacin) resulted in less than half the incidence of diabetes over a seven-year period compared to the general population. The incidence was even lower when compared to antibody-positive individuals who did not receive vitamin B3.
